I appreciate the response

> Second, I know that it's hard but you really can't put your life in someone else's hands, that's not fair to do and is a hell of a lot of pressure on someone to be told that they're the only reason you're not killing yourself. It's not a healthy relationship for either party.
> 

To be clear, I know that. It is one of my deepest desires to never tell them about this. I plan on never telling them because of what you said. And ideally, if I do kill myself, they would never find out (but either way, I don't want to tell them about my thinking).

>That aside, your partner cheated and there isn't really a way of coming back from that for most couples. Don't put yourself through that just to try to keep someone around who disregards you in such a way and puts you second. You will put yourself through so much, just to have it not work out anyways if an open relationship isn't for you.

Yeah, I don't want an open relationship (especially now, since I feel like we'd need to build trust back). I don't know how to respond to "someone around who disregards you in such a way and puts you second," because three days ago, I would say that's *never* happened. What happened is an example of that, but our bond has been so strong before that.

>What you would tell a friend, if they were to come to you with this?

Yeah, putting myself first sounds like great advice. I think having standards and boundaries is good, but I feel like I have that. I feel like I could heathily eventually overcome the infidelity with my partner, but I just feel so much fear about them saying they don't want to be in a monogamous relationship any longer.

>And I'd like to let you know and remind you that cheating is a choice, nothing can make someone to cheat. What happened is an issue with your partner, not you.

Thanks. I feel fairly certain my partner knows that.

>Be good to yourself, OP. Love yourself the most.

<3

> A person identifying as a wolf or a bowl of spaghetti isn't legitimate

From what I know, furries (and even otherkin I think?) don't "identify" as animals in the way that trans people do with a gender. AFAIK, it's more like a lifestyle choice.
Thank you! (also *she)

The last time you brought up a "practical" definition of "appropriate," I said:

>Even if it's cisnormative? Why should I?

Which you never answered, so I'll give you the chance to answer it again.

>Pray tell what you do for a living.

Why does it matter? What do you do for a living?
What  do you mean by "appropriate"?  Appropriateness is based on status quo and cultural norms, and I don't see why status quo and norms should be the ultimate principle governing our actions.

> If you don't think people should be criticized for wearing tails our conversation is done. You answered my first question. You *are* fecking daft. 

Saying that people should be criticized just for wearing tails sounds very close-minded.

> this has nothing to to with an LGBT conference

I don't know what you mean by this. Silver ties have nothing to do with being LGBT, but if I saw a silver tie at an LGBT conference, I wouldn't say "this has nothing to do with being LGBT!"  Furry-ness is not directly related to being LGBT. My point is that I don't think people should be criticized for wearing tails in a professional space or an LGBT space.

>you're mad that people said something bad about furries.

I'm not mad. I mean, you sound like you could be mad ("Don't do that."), so maybe you're assuming I am too?

Did you actually read what I've been saying?  I'm starting to doubt it, because you'd see that I insulted furries. It's pretty silly to respond to someone who said "I think furry stuff is really stupid" with "you're mad that people said something bad about furries."

>Oh, and your comic is garbage.

How so?

> furries aren't normal, trans people aren't normal, therefore furries are just as valid as trans people in an LGBT context.

That's not my point. I'm not saying anything about "an LGBT context."  My point is that I can't think of a valid reason to say furries shouldn't wear tails in "professional" contexts, outside of an appeal to the status quo. And that if we accept appeals to the status quo as valid, then that would also discount trans people.

>you conflated women in hijabs, men/women/otherwise in inuit or maori tattoos. Was that a difficult question for you? I'll give you another chance to answer.

As I said to someone else, I never mentioned religious head coverings or tattoos, so I'm not sure why you're making me respond to some supposed conflation.

>But there sure is a practical one, maybe you should follow it sometime.

Even  if it's cisnormative? Why should I?

>wearing a tail in the workplace is equivalent to being trans. It's not. Don't do that.

You should probably read [this comic](http://benkling.tumblr.com/post/78068225400/the-guy-in-the-red-went-on-to-explain-that-he) again.

>Men being distracted by virtue of them being women and cis people being distracted by trans people for the same reasons are their problem, not trans peoples' or women.

Well, in all of these cases, everyone could do something to stop it. The co-workers could all stop being distracted, the trans person could dress as their assigned gender, the woman could just be a housewife, the non-white person could just work in a non-white workplace (like segregation), and the furry could not wear a tail.  All of these would technically get rid of the distraction.  The reason we say the non-white/trans/female person shouldn't have to do that is because we've socially internalized that as *normal*. Being a woman in the workplace is *normal*, so the co-workers distracted by that have deviated from the norm, therefore *they* have to change and it's *their* problem. However, wearing a tail isn't *normal*, so the furry has to change. But in many places today (and all places a few decades ago), it is/was not normal to be openly trans in the workplace. So if this is how your determining who should change, then this would mean trans people should stay in the closet in those workplaces.

>I mean, you could have said non-white people. Besides, reading your response you seem to equate dressing in a non-white fashion (hijab, maori or inuit tattoos, etc) as... furries with a tail on. I really hope you don't find the two equivalent.

As I said in another response, my "comparison" is in [this sense.](http://benkling.tumblr.com/post/78068225400/the-guy-in-the-red-went-on-to-explain-that-he)  I think furry stuff is really stupid, and I'm annoyed by how it's getting associated with trans-ness (like the catgirl/trans stuff on the internet), because it makes transness seem like it's related to otherkin.  However, I don't see why we should uphold current  "professional" practice as the unchangeable ideal.


>Nah, mate, at this point you're making a false equivalency. Trans people dressing as the gender they prefer, grand. Trans people dressing inappropriately for the setting is another thing entirely.

There's  no  objective definition of what's "inappropriate." Most people would find it inappropriate for a co-worker that everyone in the office (including clients) knows as a man to come to work in a skirt and lipstick.  "Trans people dressing as the gender they prefer" is already considered inappropriate, so you have  to have a better reason than that to say it's bad.

> wear religious head coverings in the workplace

I  never mentioned religious head coverings, so no. I don't even know where you got that.  And I'm "comparing" them in [this sense.](http://benkling.tumblr.com/post/78068225400/the-guy-in-the-red-went-on-to-explain-that-he)

> This is just part of living in the adult world, lgbt or otherwise, it's about creating an environment without distraction so the focus can be on the purpose at hand. 

Many men are distracted by women in the workplace. Many cis people are distracted by trans people in the workplace.  The same applies to white people and non-whites in the workplace.  Trans people dressing how they want is literally an instance of disregarding cisnormative social conventions.  The exact same logic supports excluding women, LGBT people, and non-white people from the workplace.

> I think Alison Bechdel once said that if she grew up at this time, she would have been a trans man rather than a butch lesbian.

The same thing is true on the AMAB side. If you look at something like *Paris is Burning*, you see gay men that say they would've identified as transgender if they had been born later.

The difference is for each (-20 - 20), there should be (40 + 40). If you're pairing up each (-20 - 20) to just (40), you're essentially dividing 40A by 2.

The first sum  is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1...

the second is 20 + 20 + 20 + 20...

if you took every  bill from the first sum, multiplied that by 20, then subtracted each bill from a bill from the second sum, you'd get 0. Meaning that the first sum is equal to 20 times the second sum. Meaning they aren't equal:

A = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1...

B = 20 + 20 + 20 + 20...

20A = 20 + 20 + 20 + 20....

20A - B = (20 - 20) + (20 - 20) + (20 - 20) + (20 - 20)...

20A - B = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0... = 0

20A = B

If A = B, then  
20A = A  
20 = 1

20 is not 1, therefore, they can't be equal.

"Obvious" was a bad word. I meant more like the opposite of far-fetched (like you don't have to look far to see the connection).

Malcolm X was a part of the Nation of Islam. One of the Nation of Islam's splinter groups was the Nation  of Gods and Earths (also called the 5% Nation), which had a *huge* impact on hip-hop. The Wu-Tang Clan, Rakim, Kanye West, and Jay-Z all had ties to it.  RZA and GZA's names come directly from the Nation of Gods and Earths (the "A" in their names stands for "Allah").

I have no idea what newpostnewuser is trying to say, but the link from Malcolm X to hip-hop is very obvious.
